`view` takes a name or an id, as for `add section`. `at` is the marker's point on the plan `view`. The marker stands outside the face and faces the building: a marker north of it facing south is the north elevation. A marker placed over another is moved clear and a note gives where it stands. A view that is not a plan is refused in the tool's words.

`add drafting view`: needs nothing. May take name, scale.
Example:

    op:add drafting view name="Roof Junction" scale=1:10

With no name or scale the New Drafting View dialog's own stand; one it refuses is a red line.

`add legend`: needs nothing. May take name, scale.

`add 3d view`: needs nothing. May take name.
Example:

    op:add 3d view

The templates hold one 3D View, so nothing is written, `made` is empty and the note names the view; the line is green. Look with `view_activate {"view":"{3D}"}` (part 6, See your work). The 3D view is named `{3D}` in `view_activate`; its id is `view-3d` (`element_get`, `op:set`).

`set view`: needs view. At least one of hide, show, map.
Level and grid lines in a live 3D view are hidden with `hide=Levels,Grids`; the black lines labelled Roof, Level 1 and Ground were gone from the picture:

    ops_run {"name":"hide level lines in 3D","lines":["op:set view view=view-3d hide=Levels,Grids"]}

More examples:

    op:set view view=view-3d hide=Levels,Grids map=plain:lightgrey
    op:set view view="Level 8 Plan" show=Grids

- `hide` and `show` take category names. A category hide takes whole categories (`hide="Structural Framing,Structural Columns"` hid every mark and every beam). A name that is no category is refused: `no category named Braces in the Visibility/Graphics`. A view filter hides one kind of member: steps, part 5 (Commands, steps and dialogs).
- Scale and detail are rows of the view, written with `set`: `op:set id=<view id> key=Scale value=1:200` and `op:set id=<view id> key="Detail Level" value=Coarse`. If `op:set` of a view answers `no such row`, press the Attributes palette instead (`dock:Properties`, part 5).
- A view's own rows are read with `element_get {"id":"view-3d"}`; `op:set id=view-3d key="Section Box" value=no` writes one, where `param_set` refuses a view.
- Commands for views no op line reaches: `views-autosections`.

### Sheets, viewports, schedules and printing: add sheet, place view, add schedule, print sheets

Order that played: finish the model; make views and set their scale; put the annotation on each view (`view_activate` it first); then make sheets and place the views. Annotating after placing also played. The whole drawing set as a recipe: part 14 (Recipes).

`add sheet`: needs nothing. May take number, name, titleblock.
Example:

    op:add sheet number=A104 name="Level 8 Plan" titleblock=A1

`titleblock` is A0 to A4, ANSI_B to ANSI_E, ARCH_C to ARCH_E1 or None. A number that exists is refused: the Architectural template holds sheets A000, A100 to A103, A201, A301, A501, and the schedules Door Schedule, Window Schedule and Room Schedule on sheet A501 (columns of the Door Schedule: Mark, Level, Family (heading Block), Type, Width, Height, Fire Rating). Give a new schedule a name the template does not hold. The title block prints the project name from Project Information, a dialog (part 5).

`place view`: needs view, sheet. May take at (sheetpoint), title, scale, crop (pair), table_width (mm), text_size (mm).
Example:

    op:place view view="Level 8 Plan" sheet=A104 at=(115,140)

- `view` is a name or id (place by the `made` id, not by a name the template holds: the Ground and Level 1 floor plans share a name with a ceiling plan). `sheet` is a sheet's id or number. `title` defaults to the view's own name.
- The frame is the view's own size at its own scale. Two frames overlap if you do not space them, and a big model runs off the sheet. The crop belongs to the view, so one plan takes one crop: make one plan each for two buildings.
- A plan sits on one sheet. When a sheet holds it, `op:remove view view="Site Plan" sheet=A100` first, else `view already on a sheet: A100`.
- A schedule or legend is placed the same way with `table_width=420 text_size=3.5` (mm).

`remove view`: needs nothing by itself. Exactly one of view, id (ids). All or none of view, sheet.
Example:

    op:remove view view="Site Plan" sheet=A100

`delete sheet`: needs sheet.
Example:

    op:delete sheet sheet=A104

The sheet's views stand unplaced.

`add schedule`: needs category, fields. May take name, sortby, groupby, filter, itemize (yesno).
Example:

    op:add schedule category="Structural Columns" fields=Type,Count,Length name="Column Schedule by Type" itemize=no

`itemize=no` gives one row a type; left out, one row an element (528 rows for 528 columns). Read it with `schedule_read {"view":"Column Schedule by Type"}`.

`print sheets`: needs path.

### Annotation: add text, add dimension, add dimension chain, add tag, add symbol, add detail line, add filled region, add insulation

`add text`: needs at (point), view, text. May take type, leader_to (point), width (mm).
Example:

    op:add text at=(0,-10) view="General Notes" text="1. All dimensions are in millimetres."

`text` is the words; `leader_to` is the leader's point; `width` is the wrap width on paper in mm, 0 or more; `type` is a text type (default: the Text tool's). Notes in a drafting view went a line every 8 mm down; place that view on the sheet.

`add dimension`: needs from (point), to (point), view. May take offset (mm).

`add dimension chain`: needs points (points), view, offset (mm).
Example:

    op:add dimension chain points=(0,-1000) (8400,-1000) (16800,-1000) view=<plan id> offset=-3000

Each point must fall on a live element, a grid line in practice. A point past a grid's end answers `a dimension string reference found no live element within this command's own tolerance of (8400, -5000)`. A chain takes elements, not level lines. `commands_run {"name":"annotate-autodim"}` with the plan active draws the grid strings in one command.

`add tag`: needs id, view. May take leader (yesno).
Example:

    op:add tag id=<element id> view=<plan id> leader=no

One element a line; batch as the first piece says. All of a kind: `view_activate` the plan, then `commands_run {"name":"Tag All","points":[[16800,12600]]}` with ONE point inside the plan; always give the point.

`add symbol`: needs at (point), view. May take symbol, rotation (degrees).
Example:

    op:add symbol at=(-9000,30000) view=<plan id>

A north arrow in model mm; put it inside the crop.

`add detail line`: needs points (points), view. May take style.

`add filled region`: needs boundary (polygon), view. May take type, pattern.

`add insulation`: needs from (point), to (point), view. May take width (mm).

### Materials and types: add material, set material, the Material row, type_set and glass walls

`add material`: needs nothing. May take name, from, library.
Example:

    op:add material name="Blue-Grey Glass"

Example with a library set:

    op:add material library=copper name="Play Copper"

`set material`: needs name, key, value.
Examples:

    op:set material name="Play White" key=render_colour value=#f4f1ea
    op:set material name="Play White" key=glow value=0.2

- One key a line. Keys that reach the Realistic view: `texture`, `texture_size` (mm), `texture_rotation`, `render_colour`, `roughness`, `metallic`, `bump`, `transparency`, `glow`. `shading_colour` was played too. A wrong key is refused and lists the 33 keys a material keeps. `op:set material name="Play White" key=zzz value=1` answered:

        cannot proceed: a material keeps no 'zzz' (its keys: density, elastic_modulus, poisson_ratio, yield_strength, rigidity_modulus, tensile_strength, compressive_strength, thermal_expansion, heat_conductivity, render_colour, texture, texture_size, texture_rotation, roughness, metallic, bump, transparency, glow, relief_depth, relief_shadow, height_gain, cut_pattern, surface_pattern, shading_colour, surface_pattern_angle, surface_pattern_follows, description, material_class, material_keynote, material_mark, material_comments, manufacturer, cost)

- `library=<set>` adds one of the 67 shipped texture sets with its ready-made graph. A set name is lower case with `_`. A set the library does not hold is refused: `cannot proceed: the library holds no texture set named 'zinc_standing_seam'; nothing was written`. Sets are photographs and show in their own colours; `render_colour` does not change them, except nine sets that draw brightness only (lawn_mown, roof_tile_concrete, paving_stone, box_profile, precast_panel, brick_grey, brick_cream, steel_plate_painted, steel_sheet_worn). Names, graphs and the repeat of a texture: part 7 (Materials, textures and the material node graph).
- Pale materials go grey on faces away from the sun: `glow` 0.2 to 0.45 keeps them pale.

The Material row of an element carries the texture. `op:set id=<id,id,...> key=Material value="<file material>"` worked on block categories, doors and windows. A Form takes the row too (`element_get` then shows `"Material":"Play White"`). With no Material set a block takes its category's default finish; part 8 (Blocks) gives the remedies.

A native wall, floor or roof takes its material from its TYPE: `add wall`, `add column` and `add beam` take `type=`. The Realistic view draws the material of the type's STRUCTURE layer, so set every layer to the finish with `type_set` key `Layer <n> Material`. `types_list {"category":"Walls"}` reads each type's layers. The key `Layer 1 Material` on a wall type, with its answer:

    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Generic 200mm","key":"Layer 1 Material","value":"Play White"}
    {"category":"Walls","id":"3043cea2-...","key":"Layer 1 Material","layers":[{"function":"Structure","layer":1,"material":"Play White","thickness":200}],"type":"Generic 200mm","value":"Play White"}

A curtain wall is a wall of a type whose Function is Curtain: `op:add wall ... type=<that type>`, and the wall takes its grid of panels in the same Undo entry. The template's "Curtain Wall" type reads one Concrete layer, 32 MPa, 50 mm, with no spacing entries; the glass types are "Exterior Glazing" and "Storefront" (one Glass layer, 24 mm). Played on a blank template:

    op:add material name="Blue-Grey Glass"
    op:set material name="Blue-Grey Glass" key=render_colour value=#7E9AAE
    type_duplicate {"category":"Walls","type":"Exterior Glazing","name":"Blue-grey glass"}
    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Blue-grey glass","key":"Layer 1 Material","value":"Blue-Grey Glass"}
    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Blue-grey glass","key":"Vertical Spacing","value":2100}
    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Blue-grey glass","key":"Horizontal Spacing","value":3600}
    op:add wall from=(40000,0) to=(48400,0) level=Ground top="Level 2" type="Blue-grey glass"

- To put a wall that is already drawn on a new type: `type_duplicate`, `type_set` `Layer n Material`, then `param_set {"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"@type","value":"Blue-grey glass"}` (the `@type` write: piece "Change, move, copy, mirror, array and delete").
- `type_duplicate` answers the copy's `type` ("Blue-grey glass", or "Blue-grey glass 2" if the name was held) and its layers. Vertical Spacing and Horizontal Spacing are mm between panel lines. With levels at 3,600 mm, one 8,400 mm wall from Ground to Level 2 read Curtain Grids 4 and Curtain Panels 8; a second read 8 and 16. A wall per face, Ground to the top level, is one facade and one Undo step.

### Change, move, copy, mirror, array and delete: set, delete, move, copy, rotate, mirror, array

`set`: needs id (ids), key, value.
Examples:

    op:set id=<form id> key=Material value="Play White"
    op:set id="level-Level 1" key=Elevation value=3600

`key` is a row of the Attributes palette; read the rows of one element with `element_get {"id":"<id>"}` (`params`). `id` takes several ids separated by commas, so one line sets a row of elements. A key the element does not list is refused in words. `param_set {"ids":["<id>"],"key":"Mark","value":"D1"}` set Mark on one element. It refused a view.

A row that begins with `@` is an element column. `param_set {"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"@type","value":"Block 190 Core-filled"}` answered `{"changed":1,"elements":1}` and `element_get` then read the new family and type; the same call on a roof (`"value":"Terracotta Tile Battens 90"`) answered the same. `op:set id=<id> key=Type value=...` is refused: `A Roof has no parameter 'Type'`.

`delete`: needs id (ids).
Example:

    op:delete id=<made id>

The answer carries the removed id in `changed`; a floor deleted drops Floors by 1.

`move`: needs id (ids), by (movevector).
Example:

    op:move id=<roof id> by=(0,0,2700)

`by` is dx,dy,dz in mm; the roof example above lifted a roof by 2700.

`copy`: needs id (ids), by (vector).

`rotate`: needs id (ids), about (point), angle (degrees). May take copy (yesno).

`mirror`: needs id (ids), axis (pair). May take copy (yesno).

`array`: needs id (ids), count (count). Exactly one of step (vector), about (point). All or none of about (point), angle (degrees). May take group (yesno).
Example:

    op:array id=<seed> count=5 step=(8400,0,0)

- The seed stays and 4 copies follow, 8,400 mm apart in x; their ids are in `made` (`<seed>-<hash>`).
- Several ids repeat a whole row in the next direction: `op:array id=<seed>,<copy>,<copy>,<copy>,<copy> count=4 step=(0,-8400,0)`. A `step` with a z (`step=(0,0,3600)`) lifts each copy by that height.
- A frame of N crossings and S storeys is a few calls, each taking the ids the last answered: seed a column and a beam (one `ops_run`); a row each along x; the rows along y with all the ids so far; then every column id and every beam id with the storey step. Two beam rows (along x and along y) are two seeds.
- After a z step a column copy takes the level its new height falls on (a column at Ground copied up 3600 read Level 1), but a beam copy keeps its seed's Reference Level: `elements_query {"category":"Structural Framing","level":"Level 1"}` missed the copies. Count beams by category, not by level.

### Facts met in play: wall height and Base Offset, hip roofs, floors, elements_query rows

- A wall's height is its top above its level. Set Base Offset after the height and the top stays. `op:set id=<wall> key="Unconnected Height" value=3120` changes the height later.
- `op:add roof` makes hip roofs from a boundary and a slope. The `Roof` tool drew a roof from a sketch and a gable through Pick Walls (piece "Roofs, stairs, railings, fascias and gutters"; part 14 recipe (s)); Freeform Curve, Loft, Revolve and Sweep were played (part 9, Forms, freeform curves and surfaces).
- `element_get` on a floor or a room gives no `location`, so keep the boundary points you sent.
- `elements_query` answers its rows under `rows`. A real answer, first row shown:

        elements_query {"category":"Form"}
        {"category":"Form","count":3,"more":false,"rows":[{"family":"Form","id":"0da7758bd7bcd48999b9b0359b180785","kind":"Form","level":"","row":7,"type":"Form"}, ...]}

  Row keys: `id`, `family`, `type`, `level`, `kind`, `row`. `element_get {"id":"3e554d07689842945392daad3f37a354"}` answered `category`, `family`, `guid`, `id`, `kind`, `level`, `option`, `params`, `phase`, `row`, `type`, `workset`; its `params` held `{"Comments":"","Control Net U":9,"Control Net V":5,"Mark":"","Material":"Play White","Name":"","Phase Created":"New Construction"}`.
- `fields:["id","level","params"]` adds `params` to each row; `limit` is 1 to 1000 and the default 100; `more` and `next` continue. A door row read `family` Single Swing, `type` 900 x 2100; its params: Comments, Height, Mark, Phase Created, Sill Height, Width.
- A cheap check after a batch: `document_info {"categories":true}` answers the count of every category.
- A green line can still be the wrong result: read the element back.

## 5. Commands, steps and dialogs: every other control
A person can press any control UNION has. An agent presses it in one of three ways. The fast ops of part 4 are the quick route; this part is the road to the rest.

1. `commands_run`: a command by its name from `commands_list`. Use it when the input is points, options or the selection.
2. `steps_run`: a step line presses a ribbon, contextual or chrome control with picks, keys and dialog fields. Use it for sketches, typed text, draw modes, a control with a `Step:` line, and any press that opens a dialog.
3. A dialog's fields, written inside a step: `fields <Dialog title>: <field>=<value>; <button>=`. Use it for every setting a dialog holds.

Where a reference row gives a `Step:` line, `steps_run` presses it; where `Registered` is `yes`, `commands_run` presses it. A heading is the name `commands_list` prints, or the ribbon word: `draw-stair-settings` found no heading: its heading is `Stair Settings`. Look the control up (part 2); the guide not showing it proves nothing.

In this part: `commands_run`; the step language, draw modes, sketches; dialog fields; `batch`; the rules a model breaks most.

Look it up: `commands_list {"name":"Freeform Curve"}`.
`get_guide {"part":"reference > Dialogs > Dialog <name>"}`.

### commands_run: name, options, points, finish, and commands that read the selection

`commands_run` presses one registered command as its ribbon press does. Arguments: `name` (required), `options`, `points` (model x, y in mm), `finish`.

Names and options come from the command list:

    commands_list {"name":"Freeform Curve"}

The answer gives the prompt ("Click control point 1 of at least 4") and the options: `Degree` (1, 2 or 3; default 3), `Interpolate` (yes or no; default yes), `Level` (label Storey), `Offset` (mm above the level). Send an option by its Option name. The same rows are in `get_guide {"part":"reference > Commands > Freeform Curve"}`.

- `name` also finds some common trade names: `Level` answered `Storey`, `Dormer` answered `Roof Cut-out`. `Gable`, `Skylight` and `Curtain Wall` answered `count: 0`: a word that finds nothing is not a missing feature.
- Loft, Revolve and Sweep share their names with Block Editor commands (tab Make). `commands_run` by name ran the Freeform one every time.

A drawing command:

    commands_run {"name":"Freeform Curve","options":{"Degree":"3","Interpolate":true},"points":[[0,0],[3000,1500],[6000,-1000],[9000,800],[12000,0]],"finish":true}

Answer: `{"changed":[{"category":"Freeform Curve","id":"deea7bc2...","kind":"insert","table":"element"}],"text":"Freeform Curve: 5 point(s)"}`. The height comes from `Level` and `Offset`: `"options":{"Level":"Level 1"}` drew the curve at 3000. A third number in a point was accepted and the curve still drew flat: do not rely on z.

`finish:true` ends the tool after the last point. A roof footprint is finished by it, the first point repeated to close:

    commands_run {"name":"Roof","points":[[30000,20000],[38000,20000],[38000,25000],[30000,25000],[30000,20000]],"finish":true}

Answer: `{"changed":[{"category":"Roofs","id":"roof-0acc339c...","kind":"insert","table":"element"},...],"text":"Roof: 5 point(s)"}`. The roof is made from the sketched footprint. An open footprint answers `cannot proceed: the sketch is not closed -- its open end is at (30000, 19500) mm`.

A second caller is answered "another AI chat's drawing call is still running in UNION; retry in a moment": retry. While a dialog of the person's stands, `ops_run` and `steps_run` answer busy and run nothing.

**Commands that take the selection**

Select first with `selection_set`; points do not pick elements. Loft:

    selection_set {"ids":["<curve 1>","<curve 2>","<curve 3>"]}
    commands_run {"name":"Loft"}

One `Form` is written, through the curves in the order selected. `commands_run` with points and no selection answered `cannot proceed: Select the Freeform Curves to loft through, in order, then press Enter`.

Revolve: the selected profile, then two points for the axis, with a plan view in front:

    selection_set {"ids":["<profile curve>"]}
    commands_run {"name":"Revolve","options":{"Angle":360},"points":[[20000,-2000],[20000,2000]],"finish":true}

Answer: `{"changed":[{"category":"Form","id":"3e554d07...","kind":"insert","table":"element"}],"text":"Revolve: 2 point(s)"}`. With the profile selected and no points: `Revolve: 0 point(s)`, nothing written. With no selection: `cannot proceed: Select the profile curve to revolve, then press Enter`.

Sweep: the rail curve, then the section curve, selected in that order:

    selection_set {"ids":["<rail curve>","<section curve>"]}
    commands_run {"name":"Sweep"}

With no selection: `cannot proceed: Select the rail curve, then the section curve, then press Enter`.

- The prompt and UNION's refusal of Loft, Revolve and Sweep name what to select (their reference rows read `Needs: -`).
- Form Panels takes a selected form: `selection_set {"ids":["<form id>"]}` then `commands_run {"name":"Form Panels"}`.
- A cutaway box: select the elements (floor, deck and furniture blocks were selected on the house model), then `commands_run {"name":"Clip Box"}`. Switch the box off with `op:set id=view-3d key="Section Box" value=no`.

**Reading the answer**

- Its reply is `commands.run` in the reference. Check the count of what you made.
- A tool can be left standing and swallow the next drawing call's points (Form Panels did). The carrier step with `keys Escape Escape` ends any standing tool:

    steps_run {"steps":["chrome:Canvas Zoom to Fit · picks — · keys Escape Escape · fields — · expect —"]}

**A view's display style by name**

    commands_run {"name":"Shaded"}

With the 3D view in front the answer was `{"changed":[{"category":"","id":"view-3d","kind":"update","table":"view"}],"text":"ran Shaded"}`. Read it back: `element_get {"id":"view-3d"}` shows the row `visual_style` (label Display Style) = `Shaded`.

### Steps: the five parts, drivers, the options strip and draw modes, expect, typed text, sketches

`steps_run {"steps":[...]}` plays 1 to 200 step lines in order as ONE undo step. Its reply is `steps.run` in the reference.

A step is one line of five parts joined by the middle dot U+00B7; an empty part is the em dash U+2014; a fold is the arrow U+203A:

    <driver>:<control path> · picks <points or —> · keys <keys or —> · fields <Dialog: Field=value; … or —> · expect <words>

Write all five parts. Undo and Redo play in the five-part form, and Undo in the short form too:

    qa:Undo · picks — · keys — · fields — · expect —
    qa:Redo · picks — · keys — · fields — · expect —
    qa:Undo · expect —

A step to press a command is the `Step:` line of its reference row. Play that line; the word after `ribbon:` is the ribbon tab: Setout, Structure, Architecture, Massing & Site, Systems, Annotate, View, Manage, Modify, Insert, Interoperability, File or Add-Ins. A `-` means no step is listed; `commands_run` presses it when `Registered` is `yes`.

Played step line, copied exactly:

    ribbon:View:Drafting View · picks — · keys Return · fields New Drafting View: Name=Timber Eaves Detail; Scale=1:10 · expect view: Drafting View +1

Drivers (the word before the first colon):
- `ribbon:<tab>:<button>`: a press, then picks on the view. A folded sub-tool uses `›`, for example `ribbon:Annotate:Detail Line › Rectangle`.
- `qa:<key>`: Undo, Redo. One `qa:Undo` took back a whole `steps_run` call (`undid 'Add-in: steps.run'`); `qa:Redo` then `redid` it. When the newest change is the person's, UNION refuses and says to ask the person to undo it.
- `chrome:<word>`: window chrome: `chrome:Canvas Zoom to Fit`.
- `plan:<word>`: select, deselect, zoom to fit.
- `ctx:<kind>:<row>`: a right press, then a context row (`ctx:browser:Delete` took a sheet away).
- `dialog:<name>`: the fields of a standing dialog. `contextual:<key>`: a contextual-tab button (Finish).
- `op:<verb> <kind> key=value ...` plays a fast op as a step; use `ops_run` for many (part 4).

`expect` takes these forms: a count (`Walls +4`, `Floors +1`), `view Ground active`, `view: Drafting View +1`, `nothing selected`, `dialog closed`, or an em dash alone ("no expectation"). Sheets are not a counted kind: use `dialog closed`.

Picks are `(x,y)` in the ACTIVE view's own mm, separated by a space, none inside a point. A plan: x east, y north. A drafting view: its own frame. A sheet: sheet mm. Make the plan active first with `view_activate`, a floor plan by its id from `views_list` (`Ground` names a floor plan and a ceiling plan: send the id).

Keys: Return, Escape, and one key per character: letters, digits, Space, `-`, `+`, `.`, `/`, `:`, `&`. Typed text:

    ribbon:Annotate:Text · picks (0,-1250) · keys T I M B E R Space E A V E S Return Escape · fields Options Strip: Leader=off · expect Text Notes +1

A sketch tool is driven by a step: picks that close the loop by repeating the first point exactly, then a separate `contextual:Finish` step. Floor and Filled Region were played so; `Roof Cut-out` is rule 10 of the Rules piece:

    ribbon:Structure:Floor · picks (0,0) (8000,0) (8000,6000) (0,6000) (0,0) · keys — · fields — · expect nothing selected
    contextual:Finish · picks — · keys — · fields — · expect Floors +1

**Tool options and draw modes**

A standing tool ends with `keys Escape Escape`. Tool options go in the fields part as `Options Strip: <option>=<value>` (`Width=100`, `Leader=off`). A tool's draw mode (the `draw_modes` list of `commands_list {"name":"<command>"}`) is `Draw=<mode>` in `fields Options Strip:` of the ribbon step that presses the tool. Three played lines, copied exactly:

    ribbon:Architecture:Roof · picks (34000,20000) (34000,25000) · keys — · fields Options Strip: Draw=Pick Walls; Defines Slope=yes; Overhang=400 · expect —
    ribbon:Architecture:Wall · picks (50000,6000) (56000,6000) (53000,8000) · keys Escape Escape · fields Options Strip: Draw=Start-End-Radius Arc · expect Walls +1
    ribbon:Setout:Model Line · picks (50000,12000) (52000,13500) (54000,11000) (56000,12500) · keys Return Escape Escape · fields Options Strip: Draw=Spline · expect —

- The strip's fields are applied BEFORE the picks of the same step. The arc wall takes three picks: start, end, a point on the arc. `keys Return` ends a spline; the command list calls Model Line `3D Line`. A gable roof on four walls is recipe (s) in part 14 (Recipes).
- Both wall step keys are played green: `ribbon:Structure:Wall` presses `Wall`, `ribbon:Architecture:Wall` presses `Wall: Architectural`.
- CARRIER STEP: while a tool stands, `chrome:Canvas Zoom to Fit · picks (38000,22500) (30000,22500) · keys Return · fields Options Strip: Defines Slope=no · expect —` carries more strip fields, picks and keys to it without pressing it again; with `keys Escape Escape` it ends any standing tool.
- A wrong strip field lists the strip's fields: `Nonsense=1` on the Roof tool answered `fields: the options strip has no 'Nonsense' (its options: Offset, Radius)`.
- `commands_run` takes no draw mode: `{"name":"Roof","options":{"Draw Mode":"Pick Walls"}}` answers `cannot proceed: Roof has no option Draw Mode; nothing was written`. An option of another mode answers `cannot proceed: Defines Slope is in Pick Walls mode; the options strip is in Line mode.` Set `Draw=` in the tool's own ribbon step.

### Dialogs: fields lines, tables and rows, the Display Options step, settings dialogs

A dialog is answered in the fields part: `fields <Dialog>: <field>=<value>; <field>=<value>; <button>=`. A button is its name with `=` and nothing after (`OK=`, `Cancel=`). A step can open the dialog and answer it in one line, or `keys Return` presses OK.

The Display Options step, with the 3D view in front:

    steps_run {"steps":["ribbon:View:Display Options · picks — · keys — · fields Display Options: Style=Realistic; Show Edges=no; Silhouette Edges=no; Shadows=yes; Soft Shadows=yes; Backdrop=Sky; OK= · expect —"]}

UNION read back every field and answered `'OK' pressed; the dialog closed`. A new template's 3D view opens in the `Hidden` style. Realistic draws black edge lines by default; `Show Edges=no` and `Silhouette Edges=no` make a picture read as a building rather than a drawing (part 6).

**Read a dialog's field names**

    get_guide {"part":"reference > Dialogs > Display Options"}

Each dialog prints `Title:`, `Buttons:` and `Actions:`, then a table: Tab, Group, Field, Key, Kind, Limits, Choices, Notes. Display Options answers Buttons OK, Cancel, Apply; Actions Save as View Template; fields Style, Show Edges, Transparency (0-100), Silhouette Edges, Silhouette Line Style, Shadows and more.
- Write the Field column as printed (`Show Edges`, `Soft Shadows`). Kinds: `choice` (a value from Choices), `yesno` (`yes` or `no`), `number`, `integer`, `length`, `text`, `table`, `button`, `image`; the reference also prints `angle`, `colour`, `weight`, `pattern`, `tree`, `view_row`, `view_scale` and `secret`. A `read-only` note marks a row that takes no value.
- A row can carry a `name` note: Display Options prints the Field `Transparency (0-100)` with the note name `Transparency`.
- Notes such as "enabled while `shadows` shows one of (yes)" name a field that depends on another. The played step writes `Shadows=yes` before `Soft Shadows=yes`.
- Limits are `>=` at least, `>` above, `<=` at most, `<` below, `step` a whole multiple, `blank ok` an empty box is taken. A wrong choice names the items: "'System Type' has no item 'zzz' (its items: Supply Air / Return Air / Exhaust Air)".
- The heading of a dialog in the reference is the word Dialog and its key (`Dialog Import`, `Dialog Units`). The `Title:` line is what the screen prints. Played steps used both: the title (`Line Styles`, `Object Styles`, `Display Options`) and the key (`Place View`, whose title is Views). The command list can name the same dialog differently (Line Types for Line Styles).

**Tables and rows**

A table field takes a row name: `fields Fill Patterns: Patterns=Gravel` with `keys Return` and `expect dialog closed`. The row selects it.

To read a table's rows, give a row that is not there. UNION lists the rows, the step is red and nothing changes: "table 'Patterns' has no row 'zzz' (its rows: Solid fill, Diagonal crosshatch, ...)". The Place View table lists views by KIND: `fields Place View: Views=Drafting View`.

A dialog that stands needs its answer in the same step, or UNION closes it: "the step left the modal ... open: closed by the player (a window: "<title>", buttons ...; name the answer in the step's fields as `<title>: <button>=`)". A dialog-kind command opened by `commands_run` is closed as Cancel; open it by its step.

**Settings dialogs**

Opened and read by title. Rows are the first 12 UNION printed.

| step key | title in `fields` | command-list name | table and rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ribbon:Manage:Additional Settings › Fill Patterns` | Fill Patterns | Fill Patterns | Patterns: Solid fill, Diagonal crosshatch, Blockwork, Gravel, Insulation, Sand. Buttons New, Delete, Load Patterns, Save Patterns. Field Pattern Type (Drafting, Model). |
| `ribbon:Manage:Additional Settings › Line Styles` | Line Styles | Line Types | Styles: Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, <Sketch>. Button New. |
| `ribbon:Manage:Additional Settings › Line Weights` | Line Weights | Line Widths | Weights: 1 to 12; Width (mm) by view scale; Add View Scale, Delete View Scale. |
| `ribbon:Manage:Additional Settings › Arrowheads` | Arrowheads | Arrowheads | Arrowheads: None, Arrow Filled, Diagonal 3mm, Dot 1.5mm Filled, Arrow 30 Degree. Buttons New, Delete. |
| `ribbon:Manage:Object Styles` | Object Styles | Category Styles | Categories: Air Terminals, Alignment, Anchors, Appliances, Areas. |

The Detail Line `Line Style` option accepted `Wide Lines` and `Medium Lines` and read back the name. `ribbon:Modify:Type Properties` on a Filled Region opens the window "Block Manager · Filled Regions", not `Type Settings`.

### batch: several calls as one Undo step

`batch` applies calls in order as ONE undo step.

The method names inside a batch carry a dot: `selection.set`, `param.set`, `commands.run`. Played, select, set a parameter, clear the selection:

    batch {"calls":[{"method":"selection.set","params":{"ids":["<wall id>"]}},{"method":"param.set","params":{"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"Comments","value":"probe"}},{"method":"selection.set","params":{"ids":[]}}]}

Answer: `{"applied":3,"calls":[{"index":0,"method":"selection.set","ok":true,"result":{"selected":1}},{"index":1,"method":"param.set","ok":true,"result":{"changed":1,"elements":1}},{"index":2,"method":"selection.set","ok":true,"result":{"selected":0}}],"undo":"Add-in: batch"}`.

- `param_set {"ids":["<door id>"],"key":"Mark","value":"<text>"}` set Mark on one element.
- To change an element's type, `param_set` takes the key `@type`: `param_set {"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"@type","value":"Block 190 Core-filled"}` answered `{"changed":1,"elements":1}` and `element_get` then read the new family and type. The same call on a roof was played too. `op:set id=<id> key=Type value=...` is refused (`A Roof has no parameter 'Type'`).

### Rules a model breaks most (steps and commands)

Each rule came from a red step or a wrong result.

1. Read UNION's words in every answer, not only the colour.
2. Play 3 to 8 steps a call. Check each step's `expect` and the last step's `counts=`. A red step ends the call.
3. Tidy at the end: `chrome:Canvas Zoom to Fit`, nothing selected, no tool or dialog standing (`keys Escape Escape`).
4. All five parts in every step; an empty part is the em dash. A line missing parts answered "an unknown segment". The short `qa:Undo · expect —` is played too.
5. The model is the person's open model. A `start:<template>` step is red: `cannot proceed: 'New' is the person's own control, not UNION AI's; ask the person to press it`. A step that presses Save As, Open, Close, Exit, Print, Export or Import is refused with the same words and the control's name: do not retry, tell the person which control to press.
6. Take the key from the reference's `Step:` line or a played recipe; write a fold with `›`, never `>`. A guessed name is not a driver and its step does not play: press it with `ribbon:` or `commands_run`. Look the name up (part 2).
7. Quote a name that has a space: `name="Level 2"`. An unquoted second word answers "'9' stands after the kind; every other word is a key=value".
8. `expect` takes the readable forms above. A free-text expect answers "unknown expect form".
9. A dialog that stands needs its answer in the same step: `fields <Dialog>: <field>=<value>` and `keys Return`, or `<button>=`.
10. A sketch ends with `contextual:Finish`; Escape throws it away. Close the loop with the first point exactly. The tool `Roof Cut-out` (ribbon button Dormer, step `ribbon:Architecture:Dormer`; `commands_list {"name":"Dormer"}` finds it) is a sketch tool.
11. Text in a view: `op:add text at=(0,-10) view="General Notes" text="1. All dimensions are in millimetres."` first; typed keys inside a tool with no op. Circles for bar dots: `ribbon:Annotate:Detail Line › Circle`, a centre pick then an edge pick; each counts as a Line (`Lines +1`).
12. Do the plan work before you make a sheet, or `view_activate` the plan first. A sheet in front answers "Duct works in a plan, section or elevation view: a sheet is in front".
13. Pick on real geometry when a tool needs a reference: Aligned and Keynote want a pick on an existing line or element; an Air Terminal wants a pick ON the duct; a duct is two picks, and a third starts a segment Escape throws away. End a standing tool with `keys Escape Escape` before pressing another.

## 6. See your work: pictures that read as a building
Look once after a batch of writes, not after every write. A picture that reads as a drawing (black edge lines, black level lines, grey faces, white bars on a roof) is a setting of the view or a value in the model. Each cause found so far has a fix in this part.

In this part:
- `view_image` and `view_camera`: what a picture holds, widths, azimuth, `ids`, "still building".
- The Realistic look: the Display Options step and what each field changes.
- Edit with a plan view in front and show the 3D view once.
- Cutaways in the live view: the `Section Box` row and `Clip Box`.
- A picture reads wrong: the cause and the fix, one line each.

Look it up:

    views_list {}
    get_guide {"part":"reference > Dialogs > Display Options"}

### view_image and view_camera: what a picture holds, widths, azimuth, ids, still building

`view_image` pictures a whole UNION window: ribbon, palettes and model. The model is about two thirds of it. `width` 2048 was played. Its reply is `view.image` in the reference.

The UNION AI window, played. Open it with its program tile's command, then picture it:

    commands_run {"name":"gooseClicked"}
    view_image {"window":"falcon","width":1100}

Before the window is open, `view_image {"window":"falcon"}` answers `cannot proceed: the falcon window is not open; its program tile's command opens it`. What the window holds is in part 11 (UNION AI window).

A picture of the model:

    view_activate {"view":"{3D}"}
    view_camera {"fit":true,"azimuth":125,"pitch":-24}
    view_image {"window":"main"}

The 3D view is named `{3D}` in `view_activate`; its id is `view-3d` (`element_get`, `op:set`).

The same with a width:

    view_image {"view":"view-3d","window":"main","width":900}

Fit first. The 3D view keeps its earlier framing, so the first picture after writes can show the model small and off to one side, or two dash-dot lines on white. Send `view_camera {"fit":true}` before the first picture and again after the model grows.

`view_camera` takes `view`, `azimuth`, `pitch`, `fit` and `ids`. Azimuth is in model axes:
- 90 puts the camera at -y looking +y.
- 180 puts it at +x looking -x.
- 0 puts it at -x looking +x.
- 270 puts it at +y looking -y.

A negative pitch looks down: the house still with pitch -47 stood its eye 14 m above its target; pitch 3 stood the eye 166 mm below it.

Read the camera with no angle, `fit` or `ids`: `view_camera {"view":"view-3d"}` moves nothing and reads the camera. Its reply is `view.camera` in the reference. A turn keeps the target and the distance and clears any roll.

Frame elements: `view_camera {"ids":["<id>","<id>"]}` frames them as Zoom to Selection does and changes no selection.

What "still building" means. If the model has not stood whole the answer is `cannot proceed: the 3D view is still building its model; ask for the picture again in a moment` and no picture. Two causes:
- A real rebuild after a write. Wait, ask again.
- The main window is minimised or hidden behind the UNION AI window. It builds while shown.

The call that still returns a picture is `view_image` with the window and NO `view`:

    view_image {"window":"main"}

It pictures the main window as it stands. While a tool or a sketch stands (the Roof sketch was open), `view_image` returned no picture. End the tool first, then ask again:

    steps_run {"steps":["chrome:Canvas Zoom to Fit · picks — · keys Escape Escape · fields — · expect —"]}

For a fresh model bring the window forward: ask the person, or, with a shell on the same machine, restore it with the Windows call ShowWindow(handle, 4).

The ALBATROSS trap. Once `albatross_place` has opened the ALBATROSS window and it is in front, `view_image {"view":"view-3d"}` with no `window` returns that window, not the model. Write `window:"main"` for the model and `window:"albatross"` for the graph. A window that is not open answers `cannot proceed: the viewer window is not open; windows open now: main, albatross`.

`view_activate` needs a view's id when two views share a name. The template's Ground floor plan and Ground ceiling plan do, so `view_activate {"view":"Ground"}` answered `cannot proceed: 2 views answer to 'Ground': Ground (Floor Plan, id 48660e38...) and Ground (Ceiling Plan, id 5cde2487...); name the one wanted by its id; ...`. Take the id from `views_list {}`. The template's Ground floor plan is `48660e38a721430d899d5d8a96df3bec`. An op's `view=` is refused the same way (`op:add section ... view=Ground`); `view=<id>` was accepted in `op:add section` and `op:add elevation`.

### The Realistic look: Display Options step, what each field changes, the style a new 3D view opens in

A new 3D view opens in the Hidden style. The Realistic style draws black edge lines by default, so a building reads as a line drawing until two fields are set. Put the 3D view in front, then play this step:

    steps_run {"steps":["ribbon:View:Display Options · picks — · keys — · fields Display Options: Style=Realistic; Show Edges=no; Silhouette Edges=no; Shadows=yes; Soft Shadows=yes; Backdrop=Sky; OK= · expect —"]}

Every field was read back and the answer was `'OK' pressed; the dialog closed`. `OK=` presses OK.

The dialog is `Display Options`. What its fields do:
- `Show Edges` (yes or no): no removes the black edge lines.
- `Silhouette Edges` (yes or no): no for a building picture.
- `Shadows` and `Soft Shadows` (yes or no): both yes.
- `Backdrop`: Sky.

White surfaces in shade were drawn navy before these settings. With Show Edges off, Shadows and Soft Shadows on and a plain material on the blocks they draw white. Level and grid lines across a live view: piece "A picture reads wrong".

`commands_run {"name":"Shaded"}` with the 3D view in front answered `"text":"ran Shaded"`, and `element_get {"id":"view-3d"}` then read the row `visual_style` (label Display Style) as `Shaded`. For the Realistic look use the step above.

### Edit with a plan view in front, then show the 3D view once: why

After a write the 3D view rebuilds.

So work in this order:
1. Find a plan: `views_list {}`. Activate it by its id: `view_activate {"view":"<plan view id>"}`.
2. Write in batches of 25 to 35 op lines with the plan in front. The 3D view is not rebuilt on each write.
3. When the batch is done, show the 3D view once: `view_activate {"view":"{3D}"}`, the Display Options step if the view is new, then `view_camera {"fit":true}`.
4. Take every picture you need from that one build: change `azimuth`, `pitch` or `ids` with `view_camera` and call `view_image {"window":"main"}` for each.
5. Activate the plan again before the next batch.

A live picture is a capture of the window.

### Cutaways in the live view: element_get on view-3d, the Section Box row, selection_set then Clip Box

A view's own rows are read with `element_get {"id":"view-3d"}`. Its reply is `element.get` in the reference.

`param_set` refuses a view. Write a view's row with an op line:

    ops_run {"lines":["op:set id=view-3d key=\"Section Box\" value=no"]}

`value=no` switches the section box off and `value=yes` switches it on.

To switch the box ON around chosen elements, select them and run `Clip Box`:

    selection_set {"ids":["<id>","<id>"]}
    commands_run {"name":"Clip Box"}

Then turn the camera with `view_camera` and call `view_image {"window":"main"}`. The house cutaway selected the floor board blocks, deck, verandah floor, piano, table and bed; azimuth 132, pitch -47.

With the box on, its white outline and blue handles are drawn in the picture. Switch the box off afterwards with the op line above.

### A picture reads wrong: cause and fix (edge lines, level lines, grey walls, a floating roof)

- Black lines over every edge, like a drawing. The Realistic style draws edges by default. Run the Display Options step with `Show Edges=no; Silhouette Edges=no`. A new 3D view is in Hidden: run the step.
- White walls and doors go grey on faces away from the sun. Pale materials go grey there. Set `glow` 0.2 to 0.45 on the material, for example `op:set material name="Play White" key=glow value=0.2`. Keep Shadows and Soft Shadows on and the block material plain.
- Flat paint looks dirty. Relief on flat paint reads as dirt. Do not set `bump` or a Relief card on painted materials. `relief_depth` and `relief_shadow` are keys a material keeps (a wrong key lists them).
- White bars on the roof. They are the tops of external walls poking through the tiles. Lower the wall: `op:set id=<wall id> key="Unconnected Height" value=3120`. 3120 was the value on four walls of the house. A wall's `height` is its own height in mm, measured up from its level (a wall on Level 1 with `height=2700` starts at 3000). Set Base Offset after the height and the top stays.
- A pitched roof floats above the walls (the opposite fault). The roof's base is at the eave edge, out at the overhang. Lift it by the wall height LESS overhang x tan(slope): with Overhang 400 and Slope 35 that is 400 x tan 35 = 280, so 2700 less 280. Lifted by the full 2700 the roof stood about 280 mm above the 2700 walls; Base Offset 2500 sat on them with no gap seen.
- Black lines labelled Roof, Level 1 or Ground across a live view. They are the level and grid lines. Hide them:

      ops_run {"name":"hide level lines in 3D","lines":["op:set view view=view-3d hide=Levels,Grids"]}

  It answered `"ok":true,"state":"changed"` and the lines were gone from the picture. `ribbon:View:Visibility` answered `ribbon: no button 'Visibility' on View`; the step key is `ribbon:View:Visibility/Graphics`.
- Part of the ground or the site is buried. The landscape pad stands at the lowest level whose name is like "Ground". Name the lowest site level so; the house model's was "Ground Level". If the house floor is the one level so named, everything lower is buried.
- The same tile shows on a large wall or lawn. A texture repeats, and a second smaller copy is blended over the first. An 8 m brick wall and a 12 m lawn showed the tile grid. `texture_size` (mm) sets the tile. Say it in the report as a repeat. Part 7 (Materials, textures and the material node graph) holds the keys.
- Grass, roof tile or brick draws grey. Nine texture sets draw brightness and take their colour from `render_colour`: lawn_mown, roof_tile_concrete, paving_stone, box_profile, precast_panel, brick_grey, brick_cream, steel_plate_painted, steel_sheet_worn. `library=lawn_mown` is grey until given a green. The other 58 sets are photographs and show in their own colours whatever `render_colour` holds.
- White doors, pictures and fabric look like dirty timber. A block with no Material row takes its category's default finish, and Furniture and Doors draw a grey wood grain. Set the element's `Material` row to a plain file material: `op:set id=<id,id,...> key=Material value="<file material>"`. Part 8 (Blocks) holds the rest.
- A brown part of a block draws orange. Brown material words draw orange in sunlight. Part 8 (Blocks) holds the word list.
- A wall, floor or roof shows the wrong finish. The Realistic view draws the material of the type's STRUCTURE layer. Set every layer of the type to the finish with `type_set`, key `Layer <n> Material`. The call on a wall type: `type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Generic 200mm","key":"Layer 1 Material","value":"Play White"}` answered with the layer list, `"layers":[{"function":"Structure","layer":1,"material":"Play White","thickness":200}]`.

Look it up:

    element_get {"id":"view-3d"}
    commands_list {"brief":true,"tab":"View"}

## 7. Materials, textures and the material node graph
In this part: UNION has file materials, a shipped library of 67 photographic texture sets, and a node graph on each material that keeps one. Make a material with an op line, set it one key a line, and put it on an element by its own route.

A file material holds a colour, a texture set, a repeat size, a turn, roughness, metal, bump, see-through and glow. A texture set is a folder of photographs with its own graph. The graph is a set of ALBATROSS Material cards kept with the material. Textures are photographs and show their own colours; nine sets take their colour from the material. All of it shows in the Realistic view; a new template's 3D view opens in Hidden, so set Realistic before judging a material (last piece).

The pieces:
- Make a file material and set its keys: the op lines, all 33 keys (nine reach the Realistic view), reading back.
- The 67 texture sets by name and kind, and the nine that take their colour from `render_colour`.
- Put a material on things: layers of wall, floor and roof types, blocks, doors, windows, Forms, structural members.
- The material node graph: where a graph lives, the 19 Material cards, the door's reach.
- What reads wrong and the fix: pale and grey, relief on flat paint.

Look it up:

    get_guide {"part":"reference > Dialogs > Display Options"}
    albatross_place {"kind":"zzz"}

### Make a file material and set its keys (texture, texture_size, render_colour, glow ...)

A file material is named. Make it, then set one key a line. Send the lines in `ops_run` (one undo step). A value that holds a space is written in double quotes.

A plain material:

    op:add material name="X"

A material from a shipped texture set, with that set's ready-made graph:

    op:add material library=<set> name="X"

One key:

    op:set material name="X" key=<k> value=<v>

The nine keys that reach the Realistic view: `texture`, `texture_size` (mm), `texture_rotation`, `render_colour`, `roughness`, `metallic`, `bump`, `transparency`, `glow`.

| key | sets | values |
|---|---|---|
| `texture` | the photograph set | a set name from the next piece |
| `texture_size` | size of one repeat, mm | a number in mm |
| `texture_rotation` | the turn of the texture | |
| `render_colour` | colour of a plain material; colour of the nine brightness-only sets | `#f4f1ea`, `#7E9AAE`, `#ffffff` |
| `roughness` | rough or glossy | 0.05 (glass), 0.3 (brushed stainless), 0.85 (precast; board blocks) |
| `metallic` | how metal the surface is | 0.9 (brushed stainless) |
| `bump` | bump of the surface | |
| `transparency` | see-through level, 0 to 1 | 0.6 (glass) |
| `glow` | lifts a pale material in shade | 0.2 to 0.45 (last piece) |

A material keeps 33 keys in all. The other 24, grouped by kind, are listed in UNION's answer to a wrong key (below):
- Relief: `relief_depth`, `relief_shadow`, `height_gain`.
- For drawings: `shading_colour` (`#7E9AAE` in the glass call below), `cut_pattern`, `surface_pattern`, `surface_pattern_angle`, `surface_pattern_follows`.
- Physical: `density`, `elastic_modulus`, `poisson_ratio`, `yield_strength`, `rigidity_modulus`, `tensile_strength`, `compressive_strength`, `thermal_expansion`, `heat_conductivity`.
- Description: `description`, `material_class`, `material_keynote`, `material_mark`, `material_comments`, `manufacturer`, `cost`.

A whole call, glass:

    ops_run {"name":"Glass","lines":["op:add material name=\"Facade Glass\"","op:set material name=\"Facade Glass\" key=render_colour value=#7E9AAE","op:set material name=\"Facade Glass\" key=shading_colour value=#7E9AAE","op:set material name=\"Facade Glass\" key=transparency value=0.6","op:set material name=\"Facade Glass\" key=roughness value=0.05"]}

Brushed stainless, the same shape, with `metallic` 0.9 and `roughness` 0.3:

    ops_run {"name":"Stainless","lines":["op:add material name=\"Stainless Steel Brushed\"","op:set material name=\"Stainless Steel Brushed\" key=render_colour value=#B9BEC4","op:set material name=\"Stainless Steel Brushed\" key=shading_colour value=#B9BEC4","op:set material name=\"Stainless Steel Brushed\" key=metallic value=0.9","op:set material name=\"Stainless Steel Brushed\" key=roughness value=0.3"]}

A wrong key lists all 33 keys the material keeps. The call:

    op:set material name="Play White" key=zzz value=1

UNION's answer, exactly:

    cannot proceed: a material keeps no 'zzz' (its keys: density, elastic_modulus, poisson_ratio, yield_strength, rigidity_modulus, tensile_strength, compressive_strength, thermal_expansion, heat_conductivity, render_colour, texture, texture_size, texture_rotation, roughness, metallic, bump, transparency, glow, relief_depth, relief_shadow, height_gain, cut_pattern, surface_pattern, shading_colour, surface_pattern_angle, surface_pattern_follows, description, material_class, material_keynote, material_mark, material_comments, manufacturer, cost)

UNION's own words for a set name it does not hold:

    cannot proceed: the library holds no texture set named 'zinc_standing_seam'; nothing was written

Reading back. Keep your own list of what you set. `element_get` on an element shows the name its `Material` row holds, not the material's keys. The saved file carries the materials and the Display Options.

### The 67 texture sets by name (photographs; nine take their colour from render_colour)

Write a name exactly, lower case with underscores, as `library=<set>` or as `key=texture value=<set>`. The names below are grouped by kind of surface; a `*` marks the nine whose entry says `"grain": "luminance"`.

| kind of surface | sets |
|---|---|
| Concrete (5) | `concrete_smooth`, `concrete_board_formed`, `concrete_polished`, `concrete_rough`, `precast_panel`* |
| Brick, block, stone (8) | `brick_red`, `brick_white`, `brick_grey`*, `brick_cream`*, `brick_paver`, `blockwork`, `stone_sandstone`, `stone_granite` |
| Render, plaster, boards (5) | `render_white`, `render_grey`, `plaster_painted`, `plasterboard_painted`, `fibre_cement` |
| Roof tiles (2) | `roof_tile_terracotta`, `roof_tile_concrete`* |
| Timber (8) | `timber_oak`, `timber_floor_strip`, `timber_pine`, `timber_cladding`, `plywood`, `clt_panel`, `timber_herringbone`, `timber_floor_wide` |
| Metal (14) | `steel_brushed`, `steel_painted`, `steel_galvanised`, `steel_rusted`, `steel_plate_painted`*, `steel_sheet_worn`*, `aluminium_panel`, `zinc_cladding`, `corten`, `copper`, `metal_deck`, `box_profile`*, `corrugated`, `grating` |
| Floors and panels inside (6) | `tiles_ceramic`, `tiles_terrazzo`, `tile_floor_large`, `carpet_grey`, `vinyl_floor`, `acoustic_panel` |
| Hard paving (3) | `paving_stone`*, `asphalt`, `gravel` |
| Grass, ground, rock (16) | `lawn_mown`*, `grass`, `grass_dense`, `grass_rough`, `soil`, `bark_mulch`, `moss`, `sand`, `forest_ground`, `rock_cliff_grey`, `rock_cliff_dark`, `rock_mountain`, `rocks_ground`, `rock_mossy`, `riverbed_pebbles`, `river_bank_mud` |

The 58 sets without a `*` show their own photographed colours. `render_colour` does not change them: `brick_red` looked the same at white, #B4B4B4 and blue, on blocks.

The nine with a `*` draw brightness and take their colour from `render_colour`: `lawn_mown`, `roof_tile_concrete`, `paving_stone`, `box_profile`, `precast_panel`, `brick_grey`, `brick_cream`, `steel_plate_painted`, `steel_sheet_worn`. `op:add material library=lawn_mown` is grey, because the colour input of its graph is white. Give it a colour:

    op:set material name="X" key=render_colour value=<#rrggbb>

### Put a material on things: wall, floor and roof layers, blocks, doors, windows, Forms, structural members

**Wall, floor, roof: the layers of the type.** Duplicate a layered type, then set each layer's material. `types_list` reads each type's layers first (layer 1 is the exterior side):

    types_list {"category":"Walls"}
    type_duplicate {"category":"Walls","type":"Exterior Glazing","name":"Glass Facade"}
    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Glass Facade","key":"Layer 1 Material","value":"Facade Glass"}

`type_duplicate` answers the name the copy got (a name already held is numbered, "<source> 2") and its `layers`; use that name in `type_set`.

    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Generic 200mm","key":"Layer 1 Material","value":"Play White"}

UNION's answer lists the type's layers with the material now set:

    {"category":"Walls","id":"3043cea2-...","key":"Layer 1 Material","layers":[{"function":"Structure","layer":1,"material":"Play White","thickness":200}],"type":"Generic 200mm","value":"Play White"}

The key is `Layer <number> Material`: the number counts from 1, exterior side first. To move a wall already drawn onto another type, change its type with `@type`. Send the name of your duplicated type as the value; the call as played used a type of the template:

    param_set {"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"@type","value":"Block 190 Core-filled"}

UNION's answer was `{"changed":1,"elements":1}`, and `element_get` then read the new type. `op:set id=<id> key=Type value=...` is refused (`A Roof has no parameter 'Type'`).

Set EVERY layer. A wall, floor or roof type draws the material of its STRUCTURE layer in the Realistic view, so a finish on another layer alone does not show. "Concrete Slab 200 + Tile" is Ceramic 10 over Concrete 200: send one `type_set` per layer.

**Block, door, window: the element's Material row**:

    op:set id=<id,id,...> key=Material value="<file material>"

It worked on block categories, doors and windows. On a Structural Framing block the row was refused: give the member's type its material instead (below). A block draws ONE texture for the whole element; each part's colour still comes from its material word (part 8, Blocks). With no Material set, a block takes its category's default finish: Furniture and Doors draw a grey wood grain over every part, so white doors, pictures and fabric look like dirty timber. Choose by the block:
- painted or manufactured: a plain file material, `render_colour` `#ffffff`, `glow` `0.2`;
- timber pieces: a timber set;
- roof tile blocks: `roof_tile_concrete` (one of the nine: give it a `render_colour`);
- board blocks: a timber floor set with `roughness` `0.85`.

A file material's name in a block type's material parameter draws a pale timber; that parameter takes the fixed words (part 8, Blocks).

**A Form** (a freeform surface; part 9):

    ops_run {"name":"materials","lines":["op:add material name=\"Play White\"","op:set material name=\"Play White\" key=render_colour value=#f4f1ea","op:set material name=\"Play White\" key=glow value=0.2","op:add material library=copper name=\"Play Copper\"","op:set id=<form id> key=Material value=\"Play White\""]}

A Form takes the element `Material` row; `element_get` then shows `"Material":"Play White"`. A plain colour material showed in the Realistic view. Look at the picture before you say what a Form shows. Blocks, doors and windows take a texture through their `Material` row (above).

**A structural member: its type.** A beam type takes key `Material` (the call is also in the Two Towers set):

    type_set {"category":"Structural Framing","type":"323.9x10CHS","family":"Circular Hollow Section - Hot-Finished","key":"Material","value":"Stainless Steel Brushed"}

### The material node graph: where a graph lives, the Material cards, what the door reaches

**Where a graph lives.** Each of the 67 sets has a `graph.albatross.json` beside its images (colour, normal, roughness). `op:add material library=<set>` gives the new material that set's graph.

**The 19 Material cards of ALBATROSS.** UNION's own list, in its answer to a card kind it does not hold: AO Map, Base Colour Map, Cut Pattern, Dirt, Edge Wear, Flatten Normal, Height Map, Material Output, Moss and Stain, Multiply Map, Normal Map, Pattern Colour, Real-World Size, Relief, Rock Scatter, Roughness Map, Shading Colour, Surface Pattern, Wetness.

**What the door reaches.** The tools place, set, wire and read these cards on the ALBATROSS canvas (part 10, ALBATROSS). `albatross_place` and `albatross_graph` open the ALBATROSS window when it is closed.

Placing and wiring Material cards, a Material Output among them, worked.

### What reads wrong and the fix: pale and grey, relief on flat paint

**Flat grey, or no material at all.** The 3D view is in Hidden (a new template's view opens so). Set the style, with the 3D view in front:

    steps_run {"steps":["ribbon:View:Display Options · picks — · keys — · fields Display Options: Style=Realistic; Show Edges=no; Silhouette Edges=no; Shadows=yes; Soft Shadows=yes; Backdrop=Sky; OK= · expect —"]}

Part 6 (See your work) holds the pictures.

**A lawn or roof tile that is grey.** One of the nine brightness-only sets: set `render_colour` (the texture sets piece).

**Pale materials go grey on faces away from the sun.** `glow` 0.2 to 0.45 keeps them pale:

    op:set material name="Play White" key=glow value=0.2

**Relief on flat paint reads as dirt**. Paint is a plain file material with no `texture` key, `render_colour` `#ffffff`, `glow` `0.2`. Do not set `bump` or a Relief card on painted materials.

**A lawn or ground part is buried.** The landscape pad stands at the lowest level whose name is like "Ground": name the lowest site level so.

**A block shows pale timber.** Its material parameter holds a file material's name: put the file material on the element's `Material` row instead (the placing piece).

Look it up:

    get_guide {"part":"reference"}
    get_guide {"part":"reference > Dialogs > Display Options"}

`get_guide` with part `reference` lists the reference: Commands, Dialogs, Ops grammar; the Display Options call answers that dialog's fields.

Look it up:

    params_schema {"category":"<category>"}

`params_schema` lists the rows of a category. `types_list {"category":"Walls"}` reads the wall types. A wrong card kind is answered with the card kinds by group; a wrong key is answered with the 33 keys a material keeps.

## 8. Blocks: place, colour and texture them
A block is a library family: furniture, casework, fixtures, lights, plants, people, cars, steel sections, doors, windows, equipment, and the build-ups of walls, floors, roofs and ceilings. You can place any of them, change their types and parameters, give a placed block a photographic texture, and set the colour of each of its parts.

In this part:
- Find a block (`library_list`) and place it (the `op:place block` line with every key, rotation, lifting, ceiling-hung blocks, doors and windows by `op:add door` and `op:add window`).
- Types and parameters of a block: `types_list`, `type_duplicate`, `type_set`, instance parameters.
- Texture and colour: one texture per element from its `Material` row, what a block shows with none, the played remedies, and the 67 material words for block parts with their colours.
- The category rule, doors and windows.

Look it up: `library_list {"category":"Furniture","limit":5}`.

### Find a block: library_list and its arguments

`library_list` lists the Block Database's block names of one category, including blocks that serve it. It reads no model. `category` is required: `library_list {}` answers `library.list needs a category`. Optional: `limit`, `after`.

List one category:

    library_list {"category":"Furniture","limit":5}

UNION's answer: `{"category":"Furniture","count":5,"more":true,"names":["Armchair","Banquette Booth","Bar Stool","Bed - Bunk","Bed - Double"],"next":5,"total":204}`. Send `next` as `after` while `more` is true:

    library_list {"category":"Furniture","limit":50,"after":50}

A wrong word in a call lists the valid ones: UNION's refusals name their fix and list the valid words.

### Place a block: op:place block, rotation, level, ceiling host, doors and windows

The line:

    op:place block family="<family>" at=(x,y) type="<type>" level="Ground" rotation=90 host=<id>

`family` and `at` are required. `type`, `level`, `rotation` (degrees) and `host` (an element id) are optional. A value that holds a space is quoted. `family` is a Block Database block name; the block loads into the model when it is not there. A played line, a tube section placed on the ground level:

    ops_run {"lines":["op:place block family=\"Circular Hollow Section - Hot-Finished\" type=323.9x10CHS at=(0,-20000) level=Ground"]}

The form for a free-standing block, many lines to a call:

    op:place block family="<family>" at=(4200,3100) level="Ground" rotation=90 type="<type>"

- `made` in the answer is the block's id. Keep `ops_run` batches to 25 to 35 lines on a large model.
- To raise a placed block, move it with `op:move`, by (dx,dy,dz) in mm:

        op:move id=<made id> by=(0,0,1500)

- Repeat an element: `op:array id=<seed> count=5 step=(8400,0,0)` leaves the seed and makes 4 copies; their ids are in `made`. It was used on columns and beams.
- A block whose category is not one of UNION's categories answers with words that include `load it first`. See the category rule in the piece "The category rule, doors and windows".

A ceiling-hung block (its file says host ceiling) takes the ceiling's id in `host=`; the line is `op:place block ... host=<ceiling id>`:

    op:place block family="<family>" at=(4200,3100) level="Ground" rotation=0 type="<type>" host=<ceiling id>

Read the ceiling ids first (the rows come under `rows`):

    elements_query {"category":"Ceilings","fields":["id","type"],"limit":100}

Doors and windows. A door or window block goes into a wall with `op:add door` or `op:add window`, which cuts the opening. `place block ... host=<wall id>` answered ok with no note and cut no opening: the element read back as a BlockInstance where a real door reads Door.

    op:add door wall=<wall id> offset=1200 sill=0 type="<door type>" flip=no hand=no

`wall` is required; give exactly one of `at` (a point near the wall's line) or `offset` (mm from the wall's start to the centre of the opening). `sill`, `type`, `flip` and `hand` are optional. `type` is a Doors or Windows type the model holds. Played lines:

    op:add door wall=<south wall id> at=(2000,0)
    op:add window wall=<wall id> at=(65100,8400) sill=900 type="1800 x 1800"

- `hand=yes` was written to put the hinge at the wall's end and `flip=yes` to swing the leaf the other way. Look at a plan or a picture before you tell the person which way a door opens.
- A family new to the model is loaded by one placement with `host=<wall id>`; after that `op:add door ... type=` takes its types. Delete the stray block with `op:delete id=<made id>`; for a tube section the type stayed.
- For a door or window of its own hand or size, `type_duplicate` its type first (next piece) and add with the copy.

### Types and parameters of a block: types_list, type_duplicate, type_set, instance parameters

A type holds the values every block placed on it shares. `types_list` reads the types the model holds. A family in a model holds the types that were placed. To put a type in the file, place the block once, then delete the element; for a tube section the type stayed:

    op:delete id=<made id>

Copy a type, then change the copy. `type_duplicate` carries the original's parameters:

    type_duplicate {"category":"Walls","type":"Exterior Glazing","name":"Blue-grey glass"}

The played shape, on a wall type:

    type_set {"category":"Walls","type":"Blue-grey glass","key":"Vertical Spacing","value":2100}

`type_set` of a block type's material parameter takes one of the 67 words (next but one piece). The reply says `unchanged:true` when the type already held the value. A wall type's layer takes a file material by the key `Layer 1 Material`: part 7 (Materials) has the call.

Door heights were set on the types (`Height` 2400, frames `Paint - White`). A door type's `Glazed` set true draws the whole leaf as glass: set it false when the leaf is solid.

Instance parameters belong to one placed block (a Length on a skirting run, a Mark). Write them after placing:

    op:set id=<made id> key=Length value=2400

`param_set {"ids":["<door id>"],"key":"Mark","value":"D1"}` set Mark on one element and answered `{changed:1, elements:1}`.

A key that begins with `@` is an element column. On a wall, to a type the model holds:

    param_set {"ids":["<wall id>"],"key":"@type","value":"Block 190 Core-filled"}

UNION answered `{"changed":1,"elements":1}` and `element_get` then read the new type and family. The same call on a roof was played with the same answer. `op:set id=<id> key=Type value=<type>` is refused: `A Roof has no parameter 'Type'`.

For Doors and Windows, `params_schema {"category":"Doors"}` answers its identity rows and `open:true`: the list is not closed, and `param_set` sets a further parameter by name. Read one element's parameter names with `element_get {"id":"<id>"}`.

Look it up: `params_schema {}` lists the categories that carry rows; `params_schema {"category":"Doors"}`; `element_get` on a placed block.

### Texture and colour of a block: the Material row, the default finish, the played remedies

A block draws ONE texture for the whole element. That texture is the file material on the element's own `Material` row. Each part also takes the colour of its material word (next piece).

Make a plain file material, then set the row on every block that should use it. The lines are the played shapes of `op:add material`, `op:set material` and `op:set id=<ids> key=Material`:

    ops_run {"name":"Block material","lines":["op:add material name=\"Blk Plain\"","op:set material name=\"Blk Plain\" key=render_colour value=#ffffff","op:set material name=\"Blk Plain\" key=glow value=0.2","op:set id=<id>,<id> key=Material value=\"Blk Plain\""]}

- `id=` takes several ids, separated by commas with no space.
- The row worked on block categories, doors and windows. On a Structural Framing block the row was refused. Give the member's type its material instead, a file material or one of the 67 words. The call is Two Towers prompt 12: `type_set {"category":"Structural Framing","type":"323.9x10CHS","family":"Circular Hollow Section - Hot-Finished","key":"Material","value":"Stainless Steel Brushed"}`
- With no `Material` set, a block takes its category's default finish. Furniture and Doors draw a grey wood grain over every part, so white doors, pictures and fabric look like dirty timber.
- A texture set is a photograph and shows its own colours. Nine sets draw brightness and take their colour from `render_colour`: lawn_mown, roof_tile_concrete, paving_stone, box_profile, precast_panel, brick_grey, brick_cream, steel_plate_painted, steel_sheet_worn. Part 7 (Materials) lists the 67 sets and the keys `texture`, `texture_size`, `texture_rotation`, `render_colour`, `roughness`, `metallic`, `bump`, `transparency`, `glow`.

Remedies played on one house, 548 blocks plus 29 doors and 113 windows:

| Block | File material to set on the Material row |
|---|---|
| Painted or manufactured pieces, doors, windows, trim, pictures | plain: `render_colour #ffffff`, `glow 0.2` |
| Timber pieces | `texture timber_oak`, `render_colour #ffffff`, `glow 0.1` |
| Roof tile blocks | `texture roof_tile_concrete`, `render_colour #ffffff`, `texture_size 1800` |
| Board blocks (floorboards, decking) | `texture timber_floor_strip` (floorboards) or `timber_floor_wide` (deck boards), `render_colour #ffffff`, `roughness 0.85` |

Each key is one line: `op:set material name="Blk Timber" key=texture value=timber_oak`.

- Pale materials go grey on faces away from the sun; `glow` 0.2 to 0.45 keeps them pale.
- A block material PARAMETER (Bedding, Top Material) holds a word. A project material name there draws as timber. Set it on the type: `type_set {"category":"Furniture","type":"<type>","family":"<family>","key":"<material parameter>","value":"Paint - White"}`.
- Timber words carry a wood grain: leave them off cloth. Brick and stone words carry their own pattern. Brown words draw orange in sunlight.

### The 67 material words for block parts, with their colours

Every material parameter of every block type must hold one of these words. The hex is the word's colour. Another name draws as timber. Words as UNION's table prints them:

- Whites: Paint - White F3F3F0 (matt) | Melamine EDEBE4 (satin joinery) | Laminate D9D4C7 (cream) | Plasterboard E9E6DF | Porcelain F4F5F3 (gloss) | Vitreous China F1F4F6 (gloss) | Ceramic ECEAE4 (tile) | Enamel F0F0EC | Acrylic EFEFEB | Plastic - White F0EFEB | Render DBD4C5 (cream, rough) | Limestone D8CDB4 (cream stone) | Car Paint - White F1F2F0 (gloss)
- Greys: Paint - Grey 8C8C8C | Fabric 7D8790 (mid grey-blue cloth) | Upholstery 5F6A74 (dark slate cloth) | Geotextile 5D6064 (dark neutral) | Membrane 3F4A52 (very dark slate) | Stone A39C91 | Granite 8B8681 | Concrete B8B1A4 | Fibre Cement BEB9AF | Aluminium C3C8CC | Steel 778B98 | Galvanised Steel A7B3BA | Stainless Steel C9D0D5 | Chrome DCE1E5 | Cast Iron 55595D | Car Paint - Silver B4B9BD
- Blacks: Paint - Black 282828 | Plastic - Black 2B2B2B | Rubber 222222 | Tyre 1C1C1D | Car Paint - Black 1A1B1D (gloss, piano) | PE 34363A
- Timbers: Timber - Softwood DDBB82 (light pine) | Plywood D9BD8B | CLT D8B27A | Glulam D4A45E | LVL CC9A57 | OSB C8A15C | Veneer B98E5A (mid oak) | Timber - Hardwood A9814C (mid brown) | PSL B47A45 (red-brown) | Hardboard 6E4F33 (dark walnut) | Bark 5B4636
- Warm: Leather 6B4430 (brown) | Rammed Earth B88A62 (terracotta-tan) | Sandstone CFAF7E (beige) | Clay Brick A75D40 (brick red) | Soil 7A6049 | Copper B87333 | Brass C9A640 | Insulation E3CF86 (yellow batts) | Mineral Wool D6BE78
- Colours: Paint - Red B93A2E | Car Paint - Red A8211C | Paint - Green 1F8A4D | Foliage 4F7A3A (plants) | Car Paint - Blue 1F3F7A
- Glass and light: Glass BCD5DA | Tinted Glass 6B8288 | Mirror CED7DB | Glass Block C3D9DC | Lens - Clear DCE8EC | Lens - Opal F8F8F5 (glows a little) | LED Emitter FFF1C9 (glows)

That is 13 + 16 + 6 + 11 + 9 + 5 + 7 = 67 words (counted from the table).

Choose the nearest word for each surface:

| Surface | Word |
|---|---|
| white paint | Paint - White |
| white joinery | Melamine |
| grey paint | Paint - Grey |
| blue-grey | Steel |
| charcoal | Geotextile or Membrane |
| cream | Laminate, Render or Limestone |
| black | Paint - Black or Plastic - Black |
| gloss black | Car Paint - Black |
| dark timber | Hardboard |
| red-brown timber | PSL |
| mid timber | Timber - Hardwood or Veneer |
| light timber | Timber - Softwood, Plywood or Glulam |
| brass, chrome, stainless | Brass, Chrome, Stainless Steel |
| zinc, galvanised | Galvanised Steel |
| glass, frosted glass | Glass, Glass Block |
| white china, white tile | Vitreous China or Porcelain, Ceramic |
| grey stone | Granite or Stone |
| terracotta | Rammed Earth or Clay Brick |
| leaves, bark, soil | Foliage (some Paint - Green), Bark, Soil |
| lamp glow | LED Emitter or Lens - Opal |

Set a type's word with `type_set` (piece "Types and parameters of a block"); the reply says `unchanged:true` when the type already held it, and a refused key lists the type's parameters.

### The category rule, doors and windows

The category rule. A block's `category` must be one of UNION's categories, or placing answers with words that include `load it first`. Names that answered `load it first` in play: Floor Finishes, Lighting, Equipment, Columns, Site.

Doors and windows are hosted blocks. A door block's `Glazed` set true draws the whole leaf as glass.

## 9. Forms, freeform curves and surfaces (NURBS, spline, loft, sweep, revolve)
UNION has NURBS modelling. A freeform curve (a spline) has a degree (1, 2 or 3) and control points. Loft, Sweep and Revolve turn curves into a surface: the element `Form`, which has a control net. A Form takes panels and a plain colour material.

The ribbon shows Freeform Curve, Loft, Sweep, Revolve, Column on Form and Brace on Form on tab Freeform, panel Form; the command list files them under tab `Structural`, panel `Form`.

In this part:
- Curves: Freeform Curve, the height rule, 3D Line (Model Line) and its draw modes.
- Surfaces: Loft, Revolve, Sweep, reading a Form back; panels and a material on a Form.
- ALBATROSS curve and surface cards.
- A worked sequence: three curves, a loft, panels, a material, a picture.

Look it up:

    commands_list {"name":"Freeform Curve"}
    get_guide {"part":"reference > Commands > Freeform Curve"}

### Freeform curves: NURBS, spline, control points, degree (Freeform Curve, 3D Line, Model Line)

A Freeform Curve is a NURBS curve through points clicked in a plan. It is the rail or profile that Loft, Sweep and Revolve build a surface from. The element category is `Freeform Curve`; its rows are `Degree`, `Control Points` and `Interpolate`.

`commands_list {"tab":"Freeform"}` lists 17 commands (Form Panels, Toposurface, the by-face tools and more); the curve tools sit on tab `Structural`. Look the curve up by name:

    commands_list {"name":"Freeform Curve"}

`commands_list {"name":"NURBS"}` and `commands_list {"name":"Spline"}` answered `count: 0`. A word that finds nothing is not a missing feature: the NURBS tools are the commands Freeform Curve, Loft, Sweep and Revolve.

Draw one, with a plan view in front:

    commands_run {"name":"Freeform Curve","options":{"Degree":"3","Interpolate":true},"points":[[0,0],[3000,1500],[6000,-1000],[9000,800],[12000,0]],"finish":true}

UNION answers `{"changed":[{"category":"Freeform Curve","id":"deea7bc2...","kind":"insert","table":"element"}],"text":"Freeform Curve: 5 point(s)"}`. Keep the id.

Options:
- `Degree`: "1", "2" or "3" (default "3").
- `Interpolate`: true (default) = the curve passes through the points; false = the points are control points.
- `Level` (the strip calls it Storey) and `Offset` (mm above the level): the height rule below.
- The prompt reads "Click control point 1 of at least 4".

Control points, degree 2, one level up:

    commands_run {"name":"Freeform Curve","options":{"Degree":"2","Interpolate":false,"Level":"Ground","Offset":1500},"points":[[0,-13500],[-800,-12800],[0,-12000],[800,-11200],[0,-10500]],"finish":true}

The height rule: a curve takes its height from `Level` and `Offset`. `"options":{"Level":"Level 1"}` drew the curve at 3000 (Level 1 stands at 3000 in the template). A third number in a point (`[x,y,z]`) was accepted and the curve was still drawn flat at the level: give the height with `Level` and `Offset`. Three curves drawn with `"Level":"Ground"` and `"Offset"` 2400, 3400 and 2700 were lofted into one Form.

Read back:

    element_get {"id":"<curve id>"}
    elements_query {"category":"Freeform Curve"}

`element_get` answers `"params":{"Control Points":5,"Degree":3,"Interpolate":true,...}`. `elements_query` answers its rows under `rows`.

Plan view: An answer with `changed` empty wrote nothing: keep a plan in front and end any standing tool first. `view_activate {"view":"Ground"}` answered `cannot proceed: 2 views answer to 'Ground': Ground (Floor Plan, id 48660e38...) and Ground (Ceiling Plan, id 5cde2487...); name the one wanted by its id; ...`. Take the id from `views_list {}` and activate the floor plan by it.

- The draw mode of any tool is set on the options strip inside the tool's own ribbon step: on the Roof tool the fields part `Options Strip: Draw=Pick Walls` set the mode, and the strip's fields are applied before the picks of the same step. Choose the draw mode in the step, not in `commands_run`: `"Draw Mode":"Pick Walls"` in `options` answered `cannot proceed: Roof has no option Draw Mode; nothing was written`. A spline through four picks, Model Line with `Draw=Spline`:

        steps_run {"steps":["ribbon:Setout:Model Line · picks (50000,12000) (52000,13500) (54000,11000) (56000,12500) · keys Return Escape Escape · fields Options Strip: Draw=Spline · expect —"]}

  The step was green: `fields: Draw=Spline set ... presses to the tool 4`, and `changed=Lines 0>1`. `keys Return` ends the spline; the two Escapes end the tool. The arc and the other draw modes are reached the same way: the step `Draw=Start-End-Radius Arc` on `ribbon:Architecture:Wall` (it presses `Wall: Architectural`) drew a curved wall. The played recipes are in part 14 (Recipes): (p) a freeform surface, (s) a gable roof on four walls, (t) a curved wall and a spline line.

- A spline in a drawing view is a 2D line, not a model curve: step `ribbon:Annotate:Detail Line › Spline`.

### Surfaces through curves: Loft, Sweep, Revolve (NURBS surface, Form, control net)

Loft, Sweep and Revolve each write one `Form` from Freeform Curves. A Form has the rows `Control Net U`, `Control Net V` and `Material`. Steps: `ribbon:Massing & Site:Revolve`.
